case_study_insert.main_stem: Blueharbor Seafoods (BHS) is a public limited company in the seafood processing sector, employing a workforce of 240. Founded in 2001 by the Herrera family and now led by CEO Carla Herrera, it processes and exports frozen and chilled fish products to supermarkets across four continents, using a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. BHS plans to invest $3,800,000 in the acquisition of Coralbay Catch, a rival regional processor, financed by a $2,300,000 public share issue and a $1,500,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $850,000 a year, a variable cost of $17.00 a unit and a selling price of $22.00, and currently produces 320,000 units a year. BHS faces export quality complaints and labour turnover of 19%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Export Quality Report — October 2026: The Port Calder plant processed 79,600 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.9%, down from 4.8% a year ago. Export customer complaints fell from 41 to 23 per month, and rejected export consignments fell from 17 to 9 this year. A survey of 800 overseas buyers found 57% require sustainability certification and 44% ask for eco-packaging. Average shipment time is 6.1 days. Food-safety refresher training costs $650 per employee; 33 of 240 staff are due recertification, while on-the-job coaching on the filleting line continues.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Blueharbor Seafoods as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, the sharpest rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.60 to $13.41 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for processing staff. (3) Fish landing and marine-fuel input costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, seafood-price inflation is running at 7.9%, while consumer spending on premium seafood grew 3.9% in the same period.

questions.question_text: BHS plans to fund part of the Coralbay Catch acquisition with a public share issue. Explain two advantages for BHS of using a public share issue to fund the acquisition instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A public share issue raises permanent capital with no contractual repayment date and no fixed interest obligation, unlike a bank loan whose repayments and covenants could strain cash flow precisely when BHS is integrating Coralbay Catch and servicing the $1,500,000 loan taken for the same deal. It spreads risk across a wider shareholder base, keeps the acquisition affordable alongside fixed costs of $850,000 a year, and protects credit ratings needed for future working-capital facilities with supermarket customers.

Point 2: A share issue brings in new equity investors without pledging the combined enlarged asset base as collateral and without giving any lender the right to interfere in Coralbay's operations or in BHS's export pricing strategy. For a public limited company whose share price depends on growth credibility, raising $2,300,000 through shares can signal confidence to the market, fund the $3,800,000 acquisition without over-borrowing, and keep decision-making under CEO Carla Herrera's democratic-but-disciplined board rather than passing leverage risk to the bank.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to BHS's acquisition, finance mix and PLC status.

questions.question_text: BHS wants to promote its chilled export range to overseas supermarket buyers. Consider international trade exhibitions, trade-magazine advertising, or online B2B marketing through a dedicated website. Which should BHS choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
International trade exhibitions: Exhibitions such as major seafood and frozen-food fairs put BHS face-to-face with hundreds of overseas buyers, allow product tasting and cold-chain demonstrations, and suit high-value contract negotiations typical in export seafood. Costs are significant (stand, travel, samples, shipping) and presence is concentrated on a few event dates, so results must be followed up hard afterwards. For a plc planning a $3,800,000 acquisition, flagship exhibitions in two or three markets a year are affordable and high-impact.

Trade-magazine advertising: Full-page adverts in seafood trade titles reach the exact professional audience of importers and supermarket category managers, support the sustainability-certification story (57% of 800 surveyed buyers require it) and are relatively cheap. Drawbacks are one-way communication, low urgency, difficulty standing out next to larger rivals, and weak direct conversion tracking compared with digital channels.

Online B2B marketing through a dedicated website: A professional B2B site with specification sheets, certification documents, cold-chain data and an inquiry portal is available around the clock, is measurable through analytics, costs far less annually than exhibitions, and fits the 44% of buyers asking about eco-packaging perfectly. Its weakness is that buyers may not find it without strong search visibility and direct outreach, and relationship-building in conservative food sectors still favours personal contact.

Recommendation: BHS should choose online B2B marketing through a dedicated website, supported by one flagship trade exhibition a year. The website captures the 57% of buyers requiring sustainability certification, showcases the improved 2.9% defect rate and 6.1-day shipment time, and generates measurable leads cheaply at scale across four continents. Trade-magazine advertising is rejected as the primary channel because it is one-way, hard to measure and weak at building direct buyer relationships, and standalone exhibitions are rejected as too costly and too infrequent to be the sole engine for a group producing 320,000 units a year.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BHS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BHS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade-magazine advertising and exhibitions alone are rejected as the primary channel.

questions.question_text: BHS faces export quality complaints and labour turnover of 19%. Explain two benefits for BHS of using democratic leadership to involve staff in quality improvement.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 240 employees genuine input into filleting-line routines, cold-chain checks and complaint-handling, which satisfies esteem needs and strengthens commitment. Staff who help design the checklists are more likely to follow them, pushing the 2.9% defect rate down further, reducing the 23 remaining export complaints per month and the 9 rejected consignments, and cutting the waste that flows from the Port Calder plant to four continents.

Point 2: Genuine consultation lowers labour turnover of 19% because production workers and supervisors feel ownership over decisions affecting their work rather than feeling managed by distant office rules. Lower turnover saves the $650-per-employee food-safety recertification cost for the 33 staff due for refresher training, keeps tacit process knowledge on the line, and supports the integration of Coralbay Catch once the acquisition completes. Together, the two benefits give BHS the stable, quality-focused workforce it needs to protect export customers across four continents at the scale of 320,000 units a year.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to BHS's complaints, turnover and acquisition.

questions.question_text: The acquired Coralbay Catch plant needs shift supervisors. Consider promoting existing production workers through internal recruitment or hiring supervisors from outside through external recruitment. Which should BHS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal recruitment: Promoting proven production workers into the available supervisory posts would reward loyalty, lower labour turnover of 19%, and preserve the deep product and cold-chain knowledge BHS needs during integration of Coralbay Catch. Internal candidates already understand the 2.9% defect rate targets, the 6.1-day shipment pressure and the democratic style Carla Herrera wants replicated at Coralbay. Selection is faster and cheaper — no advertising, agency fees or long inductions — and the 240 existing staff see a visible career ladder, lifting morale. Drawbacks are that internal promotions can leave vacancies lower down the line, may import existing habits rather than fresh ideas, and can cause rivalry or resentment among unsuccessful candidates if the process is seen as unfair.

External recruitment: Hiring experienced supervisors from rival processors or outside seafood firms can inject new systems, structured food-safety procedures and export-compliance expertise, and avoid depleting Coralbay's production floor during the $3,800,000 integration. However, external hires cost more in fees, take longer to reach full productivity, may clash with the democratic culture, and bring no track record inside BHS, an important risk when cold-chain failures are already visible to customers.

Decision: BHS should choose internal recruitment for most of the supervisory posts, reserving a small number of external hires for specialist export-compliance or night-shift roles that Coralbay Catch lacks. Internal recruitment rewards loyalty, halves time-to-productivity, aligns supervisors with BHS's democratic quality culture, and reduces the flight risk created by the ownership change. External recruitment alone is rejected as too slow, too expensive and too risky culturally during integration; a token number of targeted external hires complements the internal pipeline without diluting it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment approaches with limited application to BHS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both approaches in the context of BHS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of BHS with a well-justified decision covering cost, integration risk and culture.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BHS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $850,000 ÷ ($22.00 − $17.00) = $850,000 ÷ $5.00 = 170,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 170,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $22.00 − $17.00 = $5.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BHS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. BHS's managers can compare the 170,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 320,000 units to confirm the group is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 150,000 units, informing whether the acquired Coralbay Catch plant can be merged without pushing combined output below break-even.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.00 lets managers model discounts negotiated with export supermarket buyers, for example a 7.5% price cut to $20.35 would drop contribution to $3.35, letting them judge whether extra volume from a large retail contract would still cover the $850,000 fixed costs and the $1,500,000 bank loan.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $850,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set the volume targets used to check the enlarged group can service the $1,500,000 bank loan and decide how to phase the $2,300,000 public share issue proceeds during the acquisition integration.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($850,000 ÷ 320,000 units + $17.00 = $19.66 a unit) to benchmark performance against Coralbay Catch, identify waste behind the 2.9% defect rate and 9 rejected consignments, and decide whether to renegotiate the $17.00 variable cost with fish landing and marine-fuel suppliers amid the 10.8% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 170,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained in detail: First, BHS's managers can compare the 170,000-unit break-even output with the current 320,000-unit run, confirming a margin of safety of 150,000 units and giving headroom to absorb any dip from integrating Coralbay Catch without threatening viability. Second, the $5.00 contribution per unit lets managers model discounts requested by export supermarket buyers — a 7.5% cut to $20.35 leaves just $3.35 per unit, so any volume contract must still cover the $850,000 fixed costs and the $1,500,000 bank loan. Third, knowing fixed costs of $850,000 and contribution per unit supports checks that the enlarged group can service the $1,500,000 bank loan, and guides the phasing of the $2,300,000 public share issue proceeds during the acquisition integration. Fourth, unit-cost benchmarking ($850,000 ÷ 320,000 units + $17.00 = $19.66 a unit) gives a cross-plant yardstick to expose waste behind the 2.9% defect rate and the 9 rejected consignments, and to challenge fish landing and marine-fuel suppliers amid the 10.8% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BHS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has BHS's financial position improved? Which of the two ratios gives the stronger evidence, and why? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.48 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.43 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.71 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.62 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $480,000 inventories + $350,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $920,000; 2025 current assets = $620,000 + $410,000 + $60,000 = $1,090,000. CR 2024 = $920,000 ÷ $620,000 current liabilities = 1.48; CR 2025 = $1,090,000 ÷ $760,000 = 1.43. AT 2024 = ($920,000 − $480,000) ÷ $620,000 = $440,000 ÷ $620,000 = 0.71; AT 2025 = ($1,090,000 − $620,000) ÷ $760,000 = $470,000 ÷ $760,000 = 0.62.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. Current assets grew from $920,000 to $1,090,000, but current liabilities grew faster, from $620,000 to $760,000, so coverage slipped from 1.48 to 1.43. The AT line, excluding inventories, fell more sharply from 0.71 to 0.62, meaning BHS depends even more on clearing seafood stock quickly to pay immediate debts. Inventories jumped $140,000 to $620,000, sensible ahead of the acquisition but raising spoilage and cold-storage cost risk; trade receivables rose from $350,000 to $410,000 from export customers on extended credit; and cash fell from $90,000 to just $60,000. Non-current assets jumped from $4,600,000 to $7,200,000 ahead of Coralbay Catch, consuming the $2,300,000 share issue proceeds, so the group enters integration with the thinnest cash cushion it has shown. Which ratio gives the stronger evidence? The acid test is the stronger indicator of BHS's short-term solvency because it excludes inventories — stock actually rose to $620,000 ahead of the acquisition, so a stock-inclusive measure would flatter the position — and it fell from 0.71 to 0.62, confirming that the weakening is driven by cash falling to $60,000 and liabilities rising to $760,000, not by inventory growth alone.

Conclusion: BHS's financial position has not improved. Both the CR (1.48 to 1.43) and the AT (0.71 to 0.62) weakened, and the decline is not inventory-driven alone — cash fell and liabilities rose. Before the acquisition closes, BHS should tighten export credit terms on the $410,000 receivables, run down chilled inventories, negotiate staged loan drawdowns, and avoid further equity-free stretch until the Coralbay integration stabilises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether BHS's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BHS of introducing eco-packaging for its export chilled fish packs.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco-packaging answers the 44% of the 800 surveyed overseas buyers who ask for it, strengthens the sustainability certification story required by 57%, and differentiates BHS's chilled range in premium supermarket listings where consumers increasingly pay for responsible packaging. It could support a modest price premium, protect the $17.00-based variable cost economics, and improve win rates on new export tenders unlocked by the Coralbay Catch acquisition, reinforcing the $3,800,000 investment case.

Disadvantage: Eco-materials usually cost more than conventional plastic, raising the $17.00 variable cost per unit and squeezing the $5.00 contribution per unit on 320,000 units a year unless the premium is accepted or contracts renegotiated. Any failure of eco-materials — for example reduced shelf life or seal integrity in a long 6.1-day cold-chain journey — would raise the 2.9% defect rate, increase rejected consignments, and expose BHS to claims from overseas buyers at the exact moment the enlarged group's reputation is at stake.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BHS's buyer research, costs and acquisition.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in fish landing and marine-fuel input costs will affect BHS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): BHS's $1,500,000 bank loan, if variable-rate, would cost about 0.75% more, roughly $11,250 a year in extra interest, spread across a large group — a modest direct cost against fixed costs of $850,000 a year. The bigger effects are strategic: the $2,300,000 public share issue looks more expensive in hindsight, new borrowing for the integration becomes pricier, and consumer spending on premium seafood could soften beyond the current 3.9% growth. The interest-rate rise is real but the smallest of the three risks.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.41 per hour): The insert gives a 6.4% rise from $12.60 to $13.41 — a derived delta of $0.81 per hour ($13.41 − $12.60; check: 6.4% × $12.60 ≈ $0.81). Production and processing roles anchored to the floor become more expensive from April 2026, and bands above the floor typically shift as well. The insert does not state hours worked, so the annual cash impact cannot be computed precisely; however, for a 240-strong workforce the effect is material, but absorbable through overtime control, productivity from automation and the democratic staff involvement that already supports quality.

Input cost inflation (10.8% fish landing and marine fuel): Raw fish and marine fuel dominate the $17.00 variable cost, but the insert never decomposes it, so no per-unit input figure can be derived honestly. What can be shown is the percentage effect: applying the insert's 10.8% rise to the entire variable cost gives an explicit upper bound of 10.8% × $17.00 = about $1.84 per unit — more than would wipe out the $5.00 contribution per unit. The true impact is a fraction of that bound, but it still erodes the $5.00 contribution on every one of the 320,000 units, directly squeezing the gain that the $3,800,000 acquisition must deliver, and it is amplified further by the acquisition adding Coralbay's volumes. This hit applies to every unit produced and processed and cannot be re-labelled away.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in fish landing and marine-fuel input costs will have the greatest impact. It is the largest percentage threat (10.8% against the 6.4% wage rise and the 0.75% loan-rate increase), it applies to the $17.00 variable cost on every unit of the 320,000-unit output, and even a fraction of the explicit $1.84-per-unit upper bound dwarfs the impact of the $0.81-an-hour floor rise and the roughly $11,250 interest increase, directly undermining the returns expected from the Coralbay Catch acquisition. BHS should respond with multi-year fish supply agreements, fuel surcharges in export contracts, selective price rises, and tighter fuel-efficient fleet management, while treating the wage rise as a staff-retention investment and the interest-rate rise as background noise to be hedged with a fixed-rate component on the loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to BHS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BHS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BHS with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
